vignette:
He is a 58-year-old South Asian man who has spent much of his adult life doing work that requires calm under pressure. As a bomb disposal technician, he has learned to move slowly, measure risk, and keep his hands steady when everyone else around him is frightened. He takes pride in being the person others call when danger is too close to think clearly. For years, that identity feels solid to him. He is married, devoted to his family, and used to being the one who handles what cannot be handled.

The event that changes him begins with his child becoming suddenly and seriously ill. At first, he tells himself it will pass, that children get fevers and infections and recover. But within a short time, the situation becomes life-threatening, and the ordinary rhythm of his life collapses into hospital corridors, alarms, waiting rooms, and the terrible uncertainty of not knowing whether his child will survive the night. He describes the helplessness as unlike anything he has felt before. At work, danger is something he can assess. In the hospital, there is nothing for him to disarm, nothing he can control. He sits beside the bed and watches machines do what his hands cannot.

In the weeks that follow, he functions because he must. He continues to work, but he does so in a narrowed, watchful state. He finds himself scanning everything for signs that something is about to go wrong. He sleeps lightly, waking to the smallest sound, his body tense as if he is still waiting for the next bad phone call. He becomes preoccupied with images from the hospital: the child’s pale face, the urgent voices of nurses, the fear that arrived before he had words for it. At times, he is struck by a sudden rush of the same dread in the middle of routine tasks, as though his body remembers before his mind does. He notices that he becomes irritable with colleagues and more withdrawn at home, not because he does not care, but because he feels constantly braced for loss.

He begins avoiding anything that reminds him of the illness. He changes the subject when family members talk about the hospital. He stays away from pediatric wards if he can. When his child later has even minor medical appointments, he feels his chest tighten and his mind race ahead to the worst possible outcome. He hates this about himself. He has spent his career running toward danger, yet now he finds himself avoiding the very feelings that remind him of how close he came to losing his child. He tries to stay busy, taking on extra work and burying himself in routines that demand precision. In quiet moments, however, he is pulled back into memories he does not invite. He sees the child’s face as it was then and feels a surge of fear and grief so intense that he has to leave the room or sit in silence until it passes.

His wife notices that he is not the same man she has known for decades. He becomes less talkative at home and quicker to anger, though he is ashamed of the anger and rarely names it. He is also more protective, sometimes excessively so, checking on the child repeatedly, needing to know where everyone is, what symptoms are present, whether anything feels “off.” He tells himself this is just responsibility, but he recognizes that it comes from a place of fear. He is also troubled by the way the experience has changed his sense of himself. He used to believe that if he stayed prepared, he could keep disaster contained. Now he knows that the most devastating event of his life came from something he could not fight, negotiate with, or prevent.

Over time, the strain accumulates. He feels tired in a way that rest does not fix. He becomes more tense at work and less able to shut off his mind at night. He finds himself replaying the hospital days when he should be focusing on the present. Even as his child recovers, he cannot fully return to the person he was before. The relief is real, but it is joined by guilt for how frightened he was and by a lingering sense that something terrible could happen again at any moment.

He finally seeks help when he realizes that he is living as though the illness is still happening. He sees that his vigilance, his sleep problems, and his constant dread are beginning to affect his marriage, his work, and his ability to feel present with his family. What brings him in is not a single dramatic breakdown, but the slow recognition that he cannot keep carrying the fear alone.
